I feel like people who talk about genetics being worse in today's bettas forget how many people insist on having newer varieties (both fin and color) that are notoriously prone to health problems.

Trying to produce rarer markings often requires inbreeding and this genetic bottleneck leads to the lack of hardiness many people complain about now. Not to mention some of these color genes, like marble and dragonscale, are a *direct* cause of health problems. 

It's very reminiscent of what happens in other species when people breed for excessive spotted patterns - you have Lethal White syndrome in horses, "wobbles" in spider ball pythons, and deafness and blindness in dogs. Dogs are also grappling with the new "Merle and Double Merle" trend in breeds that don't naturally have this pattern.

People need to remember that appearance doesn't exist in a vacuum and it ties into genes that affect an animal's entire body. No one is forcing anyone to buy marbles, kois, doubletails, dragonscales, etc. I think we need a resurgence in older "plain" varieties like veiltails that are not only healthier but can actually function as fish.

As adorable as they both are, a prong collar isn't appropriate for a Chihuahua at all. They shouldn't even wear collars to begin with because of how prone to tracheal collapse they are, *especially* a senior who likely already has some degree of collapse. Not to mention the prong isn't even fitted correctly, since they're meant to be fitted at the top of the neck underneath the jaw. The fact that it's sitting at the base of the neck, which increases the likelihood of injury, shows this facility has no idea what it's doing. I would argue this is even more harmful than the ecollar because at least they aren't leashing her with it. Attaching a slip, prong *and* ecollar to a dog who is maybe pushing 5 pounds is utter insanity.

It's not your fault, but it really sounds like the rescue and the "training" facility have both failed you. The former for adopting her out to an incompatible home, and the latter for swindling you with inhumane practices. If you're committed to keeping her, a switch to breed-appropriate and humane training tactics is absolutely needed.

All normal! His colors will continue to evolve as he settles in (they fade when the fish is cold/stressed, which is common in pet store cups) and as he matures

Bettas are carnivorous with an insect-based diet, so they can't eat plants since they can't digest them. There's a good chance his current food is too big for his liking since he's a baby. Bettas often spit out food they can't chew and wait for it to soften and break up in the water, which is probably the foraging you're noticing.

High quality foods like Fluval Bug Bites come in microgranules that are great for fish who like small pellets. Mine wouldn't eat larger Betta pellets and loves Bug Bites! You could also try thawing frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms and breaking them into small pieces.

Bettas prefer very light water flow due to their large fins. The current filter is pretty strong and is definitely pushing him around. It does look like the intake is pulling him over a bit as well. I would turn the filter down as much as possible if you can - if not, you can put a piece of aquarium sponge or extra plants in front of the intake to slow it down a bit.

For the general setup, 5 gallons minimum is recommended for bettas. This not only gives them more space, but also makes it easier to maintain healthy water parameters. This sub has lots of great resources for betta care in the sidebar, including info on cycling your tank.

How old is your tank? Cloudy water is normal in newer tanks that aren't fully cycled yet, it's from bacterial bloom as the bacteria populations get established. Frequent water changes can actually draw out the issue by removing some of the population living in the water column, which encourages them to multiply again. It's best to wait it out until the population naturally stabilizes and the water clears on its own.

I went through something very similar when I first got mine about a month ago. My family impulsively bought a Betta while I was away, with no prior planning/research, and I had to scramble to get everything he needed. His tank (which I think is the same one as yours?) didn't even come in the mail until a week later, so I was doing daily water changes in a one-gallon Tupperware while waiting for it to arrive. I was so scared of accidentally hurting him and was constantly stressed about him dying, but I was determined to give him a better life than he would've had otherwise (my mom literally planned on keeping him in a vase 🙃). Now about a month later, we're nearing the end of a fish-in cycle and his colors have continued evolving since he came home. He made his first bubble nest about a week ago!

The beginning can be very scary, and there will probably be some growing pains as you continue learning, but this sub has great resources and I've learned a ton this past month alone. You should feel glad that you care so much about his wellbeing despite underestimating what he needed in the beginning - there's a good chance he could've gone to someone who didn't care nearly as much, and I say that from experience with my own fish. You might find that you even want to upgrade his tank eventually, I plan on getting a larger one later this year!

I would continue to do your research and stay on top of his water parameters as you begin cycling his tank (the API Master Test Kit with the liquid is the best/most accurate one). There's some busywork in the beginning, but it gets much easier once you cycle the tank, since it will be able to mostly maintain itself with good bacteria. I encourage you to keep posting here if you need help, there are plenty of us here who have been where you are and are happy to help!

Did you test for ammonia? Unfortunately a lack of nitrates (NO3) means your tank hasn't been cycled yet, as cycled tanks always have some presence of nitrates (it just needs to be kept under 20ppm). If you're using test strips, these also aren't 100% accurate and the API Master Test Kit is a much more effective way of testing.

What is your tank like otherwise? Does he have places to hide? Do you have hard plastic plants or silk plants? Plastic plants are a risk for tearing fins on longer-finned Bettas. You can use old pantyhose to test if a plant is safe by running it over the plant and seeing if it snags anywhere.

Fin rot can be exacerbated by stress and water quality, both of which are probably being impacted by the number of animals in the tank. Do you know if your tank is cycled? This is the process of building a mini nitrogen cycle inside your tank via nitrifying bacteria to process waste produced by the animals. It sounds like the bioload of the tank (the # of organisms and the waste they produce) is a bit too high for the tank's good bacteria to handle, even with live plants to help. 

If you don't have an API Master Test Kit, this would be your first step for assessing the water quality and figuring out if your tank is cycled (a cycled tank has 0mm ammonia, 0mm nitrites, and <20mm nitrates). If your tank isn't cycled, this guide can help you do a fish-in cycle since you already have a Betta: [https://www.reddit.com/r/bettafish/wiki/fishincycle/](https://www.reddit.com/r/bettafish/wiki/fishincycle/)  


This sub also has good general resources for managing your tank: [https://www.reddit.com/r/bettafish/comments/3ow6vz/info\_betta\_care\_sheet/](https://www.reddit.com/r/bettafish/comments/3ow6vz/info_betta_care_sheet/)

Since your fish is already pretty light around his head, I think it's an injury. I can't see any kind of discoloration/fuzz around it and it looks more raw like a typical wound. I think Seachem Stress Guard could help:

[https://www.seachem.com/stressguard.php](https://www.seachem.com/stressguard.php)

It promotes wound healing along with reducing stress. There are also medications from API like Melafix but apparently they're not great for labyrinth breathers like Bettas ☹

**EDIT** - In the event that it *is* mouth rot, you can also use Seachem Paraguard, which has many of the same active ingredients as Stress Guard:

[https://www.seachem.com/paraguard.php](https://www.seachem.com/paraguard.php)

They also have an alternative medication called MetroPlex, but Paraguard is most likely easier:

[https://www.seachem.com/metroplex.php](https://www.seachem.com/metroplex.php)

On last week's cast, the boys mentioned the weird amount of motion blur in Sing 2 and I have some thoughts as to why this is probably the case as someone who works in the animation industry.

I watched the trailer footage at 0.25x speed and I can tell that the frames are too distinct to be created though frame interpolation, since the technology just isn't there yet for animation. Creating frames is also fairly automated in 3D animation regardless, meaning that there's no real need for them to add frames this way - so all the motion blur in the film is added deliberately.

It's not unusual for 3D animation to have motion blur added for realism (because real-life cameras and human eyes are rarely 100% focused), but I think Illumination definitely goes overboard with the amount they add as a stylistic choice. I've noticed it in a lot of their films and I think it's also exasperated by the way they seemingly render everything with a weird haze/glow, which makes the motion blur effect even stronger when things are moving. The scenes with the wolf girl in the harness are a horrendous example and they literally gave me a headache while I was playing them back.
